items.readable_text:
Content:
A compound statement is a sentence that consists of two or more statements separated by logical connectors, such as the word "and" or the word "or."

Content:
For example, the following sentence is a compound statement:

Content:
> [MATH: P: 2] is an integer and [MATH: 2] is positive

Content:
The first statement is "[MATH: 2] is an integer," and the second is "[MATH: 2] is positive." These two statements are separated by the logical connector "and."

Content:
The following sentence is also a compound statement:

Content:
> [MATH: 7] is odd or [MATH: 7] is even

Content:
In this case, the first statement is "[MATH: 7] is odd," and the second statement is "[MATH: 7] is even." These two statements are separated by the logical connector "or."

Content:
We can express the logical connectives "and" and "or" using symbols:

Content:
- The word "and" is represented by the symbol "[MATH: \land]". Notice that it resembles "A" for "And."
- The word "or" is represented by the symbol "[MATH: \lor]".

Content:
Let's translate the following sentence into symbolic form:

Content:
> [MATH: 2] is an integer and [MATH: 2] is positive

Content:
To start, we introduce the letters [MATH: A] and [MATH: B] to denote each individual statement:

Content:
- [MATH: A:] [MATH: 2] is an integer
- [MATH: B:] [MATH: 2] is positive

Content:
Then, our sentence becomes

Content:
[MATH: \underbrace{2 \vphantom{p}\textrm{ is an integer} }_A \quad \underbrace{\vphantom{p}\textrm{and}}_{\land} \quad \underbrace{2 \vphantom{p}\textrm{ is positive} }_B,]

Content:
that is, [MATH: A \land B.]

Content:
Finally, note the following terminology:

Content:
- The statement "[MATH: P] and [MATH: Q]" is called the conjunction of the statements [MATH: P] and [MATH: Q.]
- The statement "[MATH: P] or [MATH: Q]" is called the disjunction of the statements [MATH: P] and [MATH: Q.]

items.title: Expressing Compound Statements in Symbolic Form

sections.normalized_html:
Consider the following statement:

[MATH: 14] is divisible by [MATH: 4] or [MATH: \sqrt{3}] is a rational number.

Write this statement in symbolic form using the following notations:

  • [MATH: 14]

  • [MATH: sqrt(3)]
sections.readable_text:
Consider the following statement:

> [MATH: 14] is divisible by [MATH: 4] or [MATH: \sqrt{3}] is a rational number.

Write this statement in symbolic form using the following notations:

- [MATH: 14]
- [MATH: sqrt(3)]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
The word "or" is represented by the symbol "[MATH: \lor]".

So, the sentence reads

[MATH: \underbrace{14 \vphantom{p}\textrm{ is divisible by }\vphantom{p} 4 }_S \quad \underbrace{\vphantom{p}\textbf{or}}_{\lor} \quad \underbrace{\sqrt{3} \vphantom{p}\textrm{ is a rational number} }_T,]

that is, [MATH: S \lor T.]
sections.readable_text:

So, the sentence reads

that is, [MATH: S \lor T.]

sections.normalized_html:
[MATH: 7] is odd or a multiple of [MATH: 3], and [MATH: 3] is less than [MATH: 7].

  • [MATH: 7]

  • [MATH: 7]

sections.readable_text:
> [MATH: 7] is odd or a multiple of [MATH: 3], and [MATH: 3] is less than [MATH: 7].

Express the compound statement above in symbolic form given the following notations:

- [MATH: 7]
- [MATH: 7]
- [MATH: 3]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
The word "and" is represented by the symbol "[MATH: \land]", while the word "or" is represented by the symbol "[MATH: \lor]".

Note that this sentence consists of two parts:

  • Part 1: [MATH: 7] is odd or a multiple of [MATH: 3.] This corresponds to [MATH: \underbrace{7 \vphantom{p}\textrm{ is odd }}_P \quad \underbrace{\vphantom{p}\textbf{or}}_{\lor} \quad \underbrace{7 \vphantom{p}\textrm{ is a multiple of }3}_Q,] that is, [MATH: P \lor Q.]

  • Part 2: [MATH: 3] is less than [MATH: 7]. This corresponds to [MATH: R.]

So, we can express the sentence as [MATH: \underbrace{7 \vphantom{p}\textrm{ is odd} \textbf{ or } \vphantom{p} \vphantom{p}\textrm{ a multiple of } 3}_{P \, \lor \,Q}, \quad \underbrace{\vphantom{p}\textbf{and}}_{\land} \quad \underbrace{3 \vphantom{p}\textrm{ is less than } 7 }_R]

that is, [MATH: (P \lor Q) \land R.]

items.readable_text:
Content:
Let's now consider the truth values of the logical connector "and". We have the following key idea:

Content:
> The statement [MATH: A \land B] is true if [MATH: A] is true and [MATH: B] is true. Otherwise, it is false.

Content:
Let's determine the truth values of the following compound statement:

Content:
> [MATH: 2] is positive and [MATH: 2] is even.

Content:
Writing this in symbols, we have the following:

Content:
[MATH: 2pis positive_(⏟)_(A)pand_(⏟)_(∧)2pis even_(⏟)_(B)]

Content:
or, simply

Content:
[MATH: A\land B.]

Content:
Since [MATH: A] is true and [MATH: B] is true, this compound statement is true:

Content:
[MATH: A∧B≡true∧true≡true]

Content:
In this context, the symbol "[MATH: \equiv]" means "is logically equivalent to."

Content:
Let's now consider a similar compound statement but with the [MATH: 2] replaced with a [MATH: 3] in the second statement.

Content:
[MATH: 2pis positive_(⏟)_(A)pand_(⏟)_(∧)3pis even_(⏟)_(C)]

Content:
We can write this symbolically as follows:

Content:
[MATH: A\land C]

Content:
Since [MATH: A] is true and [MATH: C] is false, this compound statement is false:

Content:
[MATH: A∧C≡true∧false≡false]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
A compound statement is a sentence that consists of two or more statements separated by logical connectors, such as the word "and" or the word "or."

Content:
For example, the following sentence is a compound statement:

Content:
> [MATH: P: 2] is an integer and [MATH: 2] is positive

Content:
The first statement is "[MATH: 2] is an integer," and the second is "[MATH: 2] is positive." These two statements are separated by the logical connector "and."

Content:
The following sentence is also a compound statement:

Content:
> [MATH: 7] is odd or [MATH: 7] is even

Content:
In this case, the first statement is "[MATH: 7] is odd," and the second statement is "[MATH: 7] is even." These two statements are separated by the logical connector "or."

Content:
We can express the logical connectives "and" and "or" using symbols:

Content:
- The word "and" is represented by the symbol "[MATH: \land]". Notice that it resembles "A" for "And."
- The word "or" is represented by the symbol "[MATH: \lor]".

Content:
Let's translate the following sentence into symbolic form:

Content:
> [MATH: 2] is an integer and [MATH: 2] is positive

Content:
To start, we introduce the letters [MATH: A] and [MATH: B] to denote each individual statement:

Content:
- [MATH: A:] [MATH: 2] is an integer
- [MATH: B:] [MATH: 2] is positive

Content:
Then, our sentence becomes

Content:
[MATH: \underbrace{2 \vphantom{p}\textrm{ is an integer} }_A \quad \underbrace{\vphantom{p}\textrm{and}}_{\land} \quad \underbrace{2 \vphantom{p}\textrm{ is positive} }_B,]

Content:
that is, [MATH: A \land B.]

Content:
Finally, note the following terminology:

Content:
- The statement "[MATH: P] and [MATH: Q]" is called the conjunction of the statements [MATH: P] and [MATH: Q.]
- The statement "[MATH: P] or [MATH: Q]" is called the disjunction of the statements [MATH: P] and [MATH: Q.]

---

Item 2 — Example: Expressing Compound Statements in Symbolic Form

Example Prompt:
Consider the following statement:

> [MATH: 14] is divisible by [MATH: 4] or [MATH: \sqrt{3}] is a rational number.

Write this statement in symbolic form using the following notations:

- [MATH: 14]
- [MATH: sqrt(3)]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The word "or" is represented by the symbol "[MATH: \lor]".

So, the sentence reads

[MATH: \underbrace{14 \vphantom{p}\textrm{ is divisible by }\vphantom{p} 4 }_S \quad \underbrace{\vphantom{p}\textbf{or}}_{\lor} \quad \underbrace{\sqrt{3} \vphantom{p}\textrm{ is a rational number} }_T,]

that is, [MATH: S \lor T.]

---

Item 3 — Question 1

Prompt:
Express the statement "[MATH: 5] is prime and [MATH: 5] is odd" in symbolic form, where [MATH: C =] "[MATH: 5] is prime" and [MATH: D =] "[MATH: 5] is odd."

Choices:
a. [MATH: D∧D]
b. [MATH: C∨D]
c. [MATH: C∧D]
d. [MATH: C∧(C∨D)]
e. [MATH: D∨(C∧D)]

---

Item 4 — Question 2

Consider the compound statement above and the following notations:

- [MATH: P: sqrt(2)is real]
- [MATH: Q: 3is negative]

Expressed in symbolic form, our statement can be written as
[SELECT 1][SELECT 2][SELECT 3].

---

Item 5 — Example: Expressing Nested Compound Statements in Symbolic Form

Example Prompt:
> [MATH: 7] is odd or a multiple of [MATH: 3], and [MATH: 3] is less than [MATH: 7].

Express the compound statement above in symbolic form given the following notations:

- [MATH: 7]
- [MATH: 7]
- [MATH: 3]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The word "and" is represented by the symbol "[MATH: \land]", while the word "or" is represented by the symbol "[MATH: \lor]".

Note that this sentence consists of two parts:

- Part 1: [MATH: 7] is odd or a multiple of [MATH: 3.] This corresponds to
[MATH: \underbrace{7 \vphantom{p}\textrm{ is odd }}_P \quad \underbrace{\vphantom{p}\textbf{or}}_{\lor} \quad \underbrace{7 \vphantom{p}\textrm{ is a multiple of }3}_Q,]
that is, [MATH: P \lor Q.]
- Part 2: [MATH: 3] is less than [MATH: 7]. This corresponds to [MATH: R.]

So, we can express the sentence as
[MATH: \underbrace{7 \vphantom{p}\textrm{ is odd} \textbf{ or } \vphantom{p} \vphantom{p}\textrm{ a multiple of } 3}_{P \, \lor \,Q}, \quad \underbrace{\vphantom{p}\textbf{and}}_{\land} \quad
\underbrace{3 \vphantom{p}\textrm{ is less than } 7 }_R]

that is, [MATH: (P \lor Q) \land R.]

e. [MATH: (R∧S)∨T]

Item 8 — Tutorial: Truth Values of Statements Containing the "And" Connective

Content:
Let's now consider the truth values of the logical connector "and". We have the following key idea:

Content:
> The statement [MATH: A \land B] is true if [MATH: A] is true and [MATH: B] is true. Otherwise, it is false.

Content:
Let's determine the truth values of the following compound statement:

Content:
> [MATH: 2] is positive and [MATH: 2] is even.

Content:
Writing this in symbols, we have the following:

Content:
[MATH: 2pis positive_(⏟)_(A)pand_(⏟)_(∧)2pis even_(⏟)_(B)]

Content:
or, simply

Content:
[MATH: A\land B.]

Content:
Since [MATH: A] is true and [MATH: B] is true, this compound statement is true:

Content:
[MATH: A∧B≡true∧true≡true]

Content:
In this context, the symbol "[MATH: \equiv]" means "is logically equivalent to."

Content:
Let's now consider a similar compound statement but with the [MATH: 2] replaced with a [MATH: 3] in the second statement.

Content:
[MATH: 2pis positive_(⏟)_(A)pand_(⏟)_(∧)3pis even_(⏟)_(C)]

Content:
We can write this symbolically as follows:

Content:
[MATH: A\land C]

Content:
Since [MATH: A] is true and [MATH: C] is false, this compound statement is false:

Content:
[MATH: A∧C≡true∧false≡false]

---

Item 9 — Tutorial: Truth Values of Statements Containing the "Or" Connective

Content:
Let's now consider the truth values of the logical connector "or". We have the following key idea:

Content:
> The statement [MATH: A \lor B] is true if [MATH: A] is true, or [MATH: B] is true, or both [MATH: A] and [MATH: B] are true. Otherwise, it is false.

Content:
Let's consider some examples:

Content:
- First, consider the following statement:
[MATH: 2pis positive_(⏟)_(A)por_(⏟)_(∨)2pis even_(⏟)_(B)]
Since [MATH: A] is true and [MATH: B] is true, this compound statement is true:
[MATH: A∨B≡true∨true≡true]
- Next, consider the following statement:
[MATH: 2pis positive_(⏟)_(A)por_(⏟)_(∨)3pis even_(⏟)_(C)]
Since [MATH: A] is true, this compound statement is true:
[MATH: A∨C≡true∨false≡true]
- Now, consider the following:
[MATH: − 2pis positive_(⏟)_(D)por_(⏟)_(∨)2pis even_(⏟)_(B)]
Since [MATH: B] is true, this compound statement is true:
[MATH: D∨B≡false∨true≡true]
- Finally, consider the following:
[MATH: − 2pis positive_(⏟)_(D)por_(⏟)_(∨)3pis even_(⏟)_(C)]
Since [MATH: D] and [MATH: C] are both false, this compound statement is false:
[MATH: D∨C≡false∨false≡false]
